Pompeii History for Sleep 🌙 A Night with a Baker

About 1 hour 2 min · Released Fri 30 Oct 2026 · Updated 9 Nov 2026 · narrated slowly for sleep

Life in ancient Pompeii, told for sleep: one calm night with a Roman baker, from the donkey mills to the first bread before dawn.

Much of what is said online about Roman bread is guesswork. In this episode, what the excavations and ancient writers show is kept separate from what we can only imagine, such as the household itself and the sounds of the night.

Let's imagine a summer evening, some years after a great earthquake shook this region, in the reign of the emperor Vespasian. Pompeii is a town of perhaps ten or twelve thousand people. That's the usual estimate, though nobody really knows the exact number. It isn't a great city like Rome, but it's prosperous and busy. Wine from the slopes of the mountain, fish sauce from the shore, and grain from the farms around it all pass through its gates. The streets are paved with big dark blocks of volcanic stone.

What about the Roman Mill Room and the Donkeys?

Let's walk through the shop and down the passage into the heart of the bakery. The room opens up into a wide courtyard, partly roofed and partly open to the sky. The floor is paved with hard flat stones. And standing on it, in a neat row, are the mills. There are four of them. Each one is taller than a man, and they're made of dark grey volcanic stone, rough and heavy. If you've seen pictures of Pompeii's bakeries, you'll know their shape at once.

What about Supper and the Household Shrine?

Above the shop, reached by a narrow wooden stair, are a few small rooms where the family lives. Many Pompeian workshops had living space like this, upstairs or tucked in at the back. The rooms are simple, with plastered walls painted in plain panels of red and yellow, and floors of beaten mortar and crushed tile. A small window looks out over the street. Supper in a Roman household was called cena. For the wealthy, it could be a long lavish meal, eaten lying on couches in a dining room.

What about Making Roman Bread: Kneading, Shaping, and Stamping?

By the time the city is fully dark, the mills have made enough flour for the first part of the work. Secundus comes down the stairs, ties a cloth apron around his waist, and steps into the kneading room. This room sits between the mills and the oven. It's cooler here, away from the fire, and the walls are lined with shelves. In the middle stands a large wooden trough for mixing the dough. Some Pompeian bakeries had something even more remarkable, a kneading machine.

What about a Walk Through the Sleeping Town?

Let's step out of the bakery door and onto the street. It's very dark. There are no street lamps in Pompeii. Anyone out at night would carry a small oil lamp in a clay holder, or a torch, or would simply walk by starlight, keeping close to the walls. The town at night isn't completely silent though. Romans often complained about the noise of their cities after dark. In Rome itself, wheeled carts were mostly banned from the streets in the daytime, so deliveries rumbled through at night.

What about the Pompeii Bakery Oven Before Dawn?

Back in the bakery, the glow of the oven is growing brighter. Secundus has raked the ashes open, and laid a bundle of dry twigs on the embers, and then thicker pieces of wood on top. The fire catches, crackles, and climbs. Soon the whole oven is roaring softly, and the room is filled with flickering orange light. A Pompeian bread oven is a beautiful piece of work. It's built of brick and stone, and it's shaped like a low dome, or a beehive.

What about the Town Wakes?

After a while, Secundus opens the door. A great wave of heat and steam rolls out. He reaches in with the peel and draws out a loaf. He taps the bottom with his knuckle and listens. It sounds hollow. It's done. One by one, the loaves come out, golden brown and crackling, their eight wedges standing up proud, the stamp pressed neatly into each one. They're set on racks and shelves to cool. Some of them will go out to the shop counter.

Over the next hour, we'll walk a bakers' street at dusk, watch the donkeys turn the mills through the night, and wait by the oven for the first loaves of morning.

This is Dreaming Ages.

If your mind is busy tonight, we are here for you with stories every week. Every element of this experience is intentionally designed to guide you into a deep sleep. We blend rich historical research with a slow, calming narration, soothing music, and immersive night sounds. Our stories offer just enough history to engage your mind without keeping it awake, easing you into a natural slumber. Don't worry about making it to the end; you can always pick up where you left off tomorrow. Tonight, wrap yourself in the comfort of a slow-paced story, the gentle glow of a clay lamp, and the soft crackle of a bread oven.

Now… pull up the blanket, and rest your head on the pillow.

Let's begin with a few slow breaths in… and some long breaths out. Feel your shoulders soften, and let each breath settle a little deeper than the last. There's nowhere you need to be tonight, and nothing more to be done.

I'll blow out the candle… Now… follow me back in time, to a warm bakery doorway on a dark stone street, where the long night of bread is just beginning.

It's a summer evening, nearly two thousand years ago, in a busy Roman town called Pompeii. We're on the Bay of Naples, in what is modern-day Italy, on a low ridge close to the sea. Behind the town rises a broad green mountain, its slopes covered in vineyards. The people who live here call it Vesuvius, and to them it's simply part of the view, like the sea and the sky. Tonight we'll spend one ordinary night with a baker's household, from dusk until the first loaves go out at dawn.

The streets, the mills and the ovens are real, and so is the bread. The baker and his household are imagined, but people very like them lived and worked here.

A warm glow spills from a bakery doorway onto a dark stone street. Inside, a donkey walks its slow circle around a millstone, and flour drifts in the lamplight like dust in a sunbeam. A baker leans over a wooden trough, pressing his knuckles into the dough.

Intro

Pompeii is one of the best places in the whole ancient world to spend a night like this. Archaeologists have found about forty bakeries inside its walls, with their mills, their ovens, their kneading rooms, and their stables. One of them, the bakery of Modestus, is where those eighty-one loaves were found.

As we go, keep one thing in mind: the glow of the oven. It's there at dusk, as the last batch of the day comes out. It's there at midnight, banked low and waiting. And it's there before dawn, when the fire is raked aside and the loaves slide in. Bakers all over the Roman world kept that glow alive through the dark, so that a town would wake up to bread. Tonight we'll keep coming back to it, the way a traveller on a cold street might turn toward a warm doorway.

Our story begins on a narrow street near the middle of town, just as the sun goes down behind the sea.

05:12Evening on the Bakers' Street in Ancient Pompeii · 1,129 words

Let's imagine a summer evening, some years after a great earthquake shook this region, in the reign of the emperor Vespasian. Pompeii is a town of perhaps ten or twelve thousand people. That's the usual estimate, though nobody really knows the exact number. It isn't a great city like Rome, but it's prosperous and busy. Wine from the slopes of the mountain, fish sauce from the shore, and grain from the farms around it all pass through its gates.

The streets are paved with big dark blocks of volcanic stone. They're worn into ruts by cart wheels, and they're lined with raised pavements on either side. Where the streets cross, there are tall stepping stones, so people can cross without stepping into the mud and water that run down the middle when it rains. Here and there, a public fountain trickles into a stone basin, and the water spills over and runs away downhill.

By now the shops along the street are closing. Most of them are small rooms that open straight onto the pavement, with wide doorways and wooden shutters that slide into grooves in the stone. A man selling hot food is wiping down his counter, where round jars are set into the stone top. A fuller is hanging out the last of the day's cloth. Children are being called indoors. On the walls, painted in red and black letters, are notices asking people to vote for one man or another in the coming town elections. Some of them were painted by groups of neighbours or tradesmen, and a few of the surviving notices are signed by bakers.

Those painted notices were often put up at night, when the streets were empty. A professional sign writer would come along after dark, with a ladder, a pot of red paint and a broad brush, and someone to hold a lamp for him. One notice in Pompeii even ends with a little line for that helper, telling the lantern carrier to hold the ladder. Tonight, two streets away, we can just see one of these painters at work. A small lamp bobs on the end of a pole, and big red letters are slowly appearing on the white plaster, one careful stroke at a time.

Not every notice was entirely serious. On a wall beside a tavern, in the same block as the great bakery of Popidius Priscus, someone painted a recommendation for a man named Marcus Cerrinius Vatia, who was standing for office. It says that all the late drinkers ask you to vote for him. Nearby, another notice for the same man claims the support of all the late sleepers. Scholars still aren't sure whether these were real support, or a joke at the candidate's expense. Either way, they're a lovely reminder that people in Pompeii stayed up late, and laughed, and teased their neighbours, just as people do now.

Our bakery stands on a corner, and it's easy to spot. Even from down the street, you can smell it. There's warm bread, woodsmoke, and the dry clean smell of flour. A wide doorway opens onto a small shop, with a counter where the day's bread was sold. Behind it, a passage leads back into the working rooms, and there, the glow of the oven is still showing orange in the dusk.

Bakeries like this one were called pistrina. A single one was a pistrinum, and the man who ran it was a pistor. The word first meant someone who pounds grain, from the old days when grain was crushed by hand in a mortar. By now, in Pompeii, the pistor does much more than that. He grinds the grain, makes the dough, bakes the bread, and very often sells it too, all under one roof.

Let's give our baker a name, just for tonight. We'll call him Secundus. It was a common Roman name, and we use it only as an example. He's in his forties, with thick forearms and a little flour always caught in the creases of his knuckles. Perhaps he was born enslaved and later freed. Many of the craftsmen and shopkeepers of Roman towns were freedmen, and some of them became quite comfortable. But we can't know that about an imagined man, so let's simply say he's worked in bakeries all his life.

His household is larger than just a family. There's his wife, whom we'll call Fortunata, who keeps the accounts and runs the shop counter in the mornings. There are two children, a girl and a younger boy. And there are the workers. In a bakery of this size, some of them would almost certainly have been enslaved people. Others might have been hired men, paid by the day. The work of a Roman bakery was hard and hot, and for many of the people who did it, it wasn't freely chosen. We'll keep them in mind tonight, too.

As the light fades, the last loaves of the day are taken from the oven and set on the shelves to cool. The bread from the morning's bake sold early, as it always does. The afternoon batch was smaller, mostly for the taverns and for customers who came late from the baths. Now Fortunata counts the takings, the small bronze coins called asses, and the larger brass ones called sestertii. Four asses make one sestertius. She stacks them in little piles on the counter and writes the totals on a wax tablet, pressing the letters into the dark wax with a pointed stylus.

Wax tablets were the everyday notebooks of the Roman world. They were thin wooden boards with a shallow tray of wax, often tied together in pairs or threes. You wrote by scratching into the wax, and when you were done with a note, you smoothed it flat with the blunt end of the stylus and started again. In Pompeii, the house of a banker named Caecilius Iucundus held more than a hundred and fifty of these tablets, recording his business deals. Ours is a much humbler set, but it serves the same purpose. How much flour was bought, how much bread was sold, and who owes a few coins.

Outside, the sky over the sea is turning from gold to rose, and then to a soft grey blue. Swallows dart over the rooftops, and then they're gone. Somewhere a dog barks, and somewhere else a door is barred for the night. The shutters slide closed along the street, one after another, until the only light left is the glow from our bakery's back room, and the small flames of oil lamps in upstairs windows.

For most of Pompeii, the evening is winding down. But in the bakery, the most important part of the day is about to begin.

13:29The Roman Mill Room and the Donkeys · 1,105 words

Let's walk through the shop and down the passage into the heart of the bakery. The room opens up into a wide courtyard, partly roofed and partly open to the sky. The floor is paved with hard flat stones. And standing on it, in a neat row, are the mills.

There are four of them. Each one is taller than a man, and they're made of dark grey volcanic stone, rough and heavy. If you've seen pictures of Pompeii's bakeries, you'll know their shape at once. Each mill has two parts. The lower part, called the meta, is a solid cone, standing on a round stone base. Fitted over the top of it is the upper part, called the catillus. It's hollow, and shaped like an hourglass, or like two funnels joined at their narrow ends.

The grain goes into the upper funnel of the catillus. It trickles down through the narrow waist and into the gap between the two stones. When the catillus turns, the grain is crushed and ground between the hollow upper stone and the cone beneath it. The flour falls out at the bottom, onto the round base, where it can be swept up.

To turn the catillus, square holes were cut into its narrow waist, one on each side. Strong wooden beams were fitted into those holes, and a wooden frame held them in place. Then either people or animals pushed or pulled the beams around in a circle, around and around, for hours at a time. In Pompeii, the work was often done by donkeys or mules. That's why these mills are sometimes called donkey mills.

At the bakery of Popidius Priscus, one of the largest in town, there are still five of these mills standing today, with a great oven nearby. At the bakery of Modestus, there were four. And in many bakeries, archaeologists have found a stable close to the mill room, with stone feeding troughs, where the animals rested between shifts.

Tonight, two donkeys are already harnessed. They have blinkers over their eyes. The Roman writer Apuleius describes mill donkeys with their faces covered, so they wouldn't grow dizzy walking a circle that never led anywhere. One is grey, with a dark stripe down his back. The other is brown and a little older, with white hairs around his muzzle. Let's imagine a young worker leading them, a boy of about fifteen, clicking his tongue softly and patting their necks.

The donkeys begin to walk. The stone grinds, low and steady, a deep dry rumble that you feel in your feet as much as you hear it. The beam creaks in its socket. The donkeys' hooves tap on the stone floor, round and round. It's a sound that must have filled the back streets of Pompeii every night, from dozens of bakeries at once.

Romans had a soft spot for the donkeys of the mill, as well as some sympathy. Every June, during the festival of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, the mill donkeys were given a day of rest. They were decorated with garlands of flowers and little loaves of bread strung around their necks. And in Pompeii, several bakeries had painted shrines showing Vesta with a donkey standing quietly beside her. One of them was in the bakery of Modestus itself. It's a small kind detail in a hard working world.

The grain being ground tonight is wheat. Most of it would have come from the farms of Campania, the rich and fertile plain around the bay, though grain was also shipped in from much farther away, from Sicily, Egypt, and North Africa. It came to the bakery in sacks, or in tall clay jars, and it was stored in a dry room near the mill. Before grinding, it was sifted and cleaned, to take out the bits of chaff, the small stones, and the seeds of weeds.

As the flour falls from the mill, a worker gathers it up with a small brush and a wooden scoop. He tips it into a sieve, and shakes it softly over a wide basket. Coarser flour, with more of the bran in it, made darker, heavier bread. Finer flour, sifted again and again, made white bread, which cost more. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder, who lived at this very time, describes different grades of bread in his great encyclopaedia, the Natural History. There was fine white bread for the wealthy, and coarser bread for ordinary people and for slaves. Many bakeries likely made several kinds.

Grinding by animal power was slow. Modern estimates suggest that a single donkey mill could grind somewhere between ten and twenty-five kilos of grain in an hour. Those are only estimates, and they vary quite a lot. But it's clear that a busy bakery needed its mills turning for many hours to make enough bread for the morning.

The stone of the mills was special too. Not just any rock would do. It needed to be hard, so that it wouldn't crumble into the flour, but also rough and full of tiny holes, so that it would keep a good cutting surface as it wore down. Volcanic lava stone was ideal. Studies of Pompeii's mills show that more than half of those tested were quarried near Orvieto, in central Italy, far to the north. Most of the rest were cut from very old lava from the Vesuvius area itself. They were heavy valuable things, and they were made to last.

Still, the grain leaves its mark. A little grit from the millstones always found its way into Roman bread. Studies of Roman teeth show that people's teeth were often worn down by it. It's one small reminder that even ordinary meals took effort, from the farm to the mill to the table.

While the donkeys walk, the boy sits on an upturned basket by the wall and listens to the steady rumble. Every so often, he gets up to pour more grain into the funnel at the top of the mill, or to scratch the grey donkey behind the ears. Across the courtyard, through the open doorway of the oven room, the glow of the oven is low and red. The fire was let down after the afternoon bake, and now it waits, keeping the bricks warm, until it's needed again.

Overhead, the sky has gone deep blue. The first stars are coming out above the roof tiles. In the stable, a third donkey shifts its weight and sighs, and settles down on the straw.

Let's leave the mills turning, and step upstairs, where the family is gathering for supper.

21:38Supper and the Household Shrine · 974 words

Above the shop, reached by a narrow wooden stair, are a few small rooms where the family lives. Many Pompeian workshops had living space like this, upstairs or tucked in at the back. The rooms are simple, with plastered walls painted in plain panels of red and yellow, and floors of beaten mortar and crushed tile. A small window looks out over the street.

Supper in a Roman household was called cena. For the wealthy, it could be a long lavish meal, eaten lying on couches in a dining room. For a working household like ours, it's much simpler, and it's eaten sitting on stools around a low table.

Tonight there's bread, of course. It's yesterday's loaf, a little dry now, but good for dipping. There's a bowl of puls, a thick porridge of grain cooked with water, which was one of the oldest Roman foods of all. There are olives, a piece of hard cheese, some onions and a few figs. There's a small dish of fish sauce, called garum, for flavour. Garum was made by leaving small fish and salt to break down in the sun for weeks, and it was used the way we might use salt or soy sauce. Pompeii was famous for it. One local producer, a man named Umbricius Scaurus, sold his fish sauce in little jars marked with his name, and those jars turn up all over the town.

There's wine too, mixed with water as the Romans almost always drank it. It's a cheap local wine, from vineyards a short walk away, on the slopes of the mountain.

The children eat quickly and yawn. Fortunata tells them about a neighbour's new baby, and about the price of oil going up again. Secundus eats slowly, and listens. He'll be up most of the night, and he knows he'll need his strength. Down below, the mills rumble on, and the sound comes up through the floorboards like a slow heartbeat.

When supper's done, there's one more small duty. In a corner of the bakery, near the oven, is a household shrine called a lararium. Nearly every house and workshop in Pompeii had one. Some were grand little temples, with columns and a painted pediment. Others, like ours, were just a niche in the wall, with a small shelf in front of it.

Painted on the wall of the niche are the household gods. In the middle stands the Genius, the guardian spirit of the head of the household. He's dressed in a toga, and he's pouring an offering from a shallow bowl. On either side are the Lares, two young dancing figures, each holding up a drinking horn. Below them, as in so many Pompeian shrines, are two large painted snakes, winding toward an altar. To Roman eyes, the snakes weren't frightening at all. They were protective spirits of the home and the land.

Fortunata takes a small piece of bread and a pinch of salt and sets them on the shelf. She lights a little clay oil lamp and places it in front of the painted gods. Then she says a few quiet words. We don't know exactly what a Pompeian baker's wife might have said at her shrine. But we know Romans asked their household gods for simple things, for health, for safety, and for a good year. In a bakery, she might ask that the fire behaves, and the dough rises, and the bread sells well in the morning.

The little lamp flickers. Its flame is tiny next to the glow of the oven across the room, but it's the same warm colour, and for a moment the two lights seem to answer each other in the dark.

The children are sent to bed. The boy sleeps on a straw mattress in a small room upstairs. His sister shares a narrow bed with him on cold nights, though tonight is warm. They can hear the mills below them, and the donkeys' hooves, and the soft voices of the workers. Children who grow up over a bakery probably slept right through it all.

Let's pause for a moment on Fortunata, and on a picture that some of you may know. In a house in Pompeii, in the same block as the bakery of Popidius Priscus, there's a famous painted portrait of a married couple. He wears a white toga and holds a rolled scroll. She holds a wax tablet in one hand, and touches a stylus to her lips with the other, as though she's thinking about what to write. They look straight out at us, serious and calm.

For a long time, this man was called Paquius Proculus, and he was described as a baker. But scholars today mostly link the house to a man named Terentius Neo, whose name was painted on the wall outside. At some stage, part of the house was turned into a bakery. So it's possible that Terentius Neo was connected to the bakery trade. It's also possible the bakery was run by someone else, or added later. We simply don't know for sure. What the portrait does tell us is how a successful Pompeian couple wanted to be seen. They wanted to look educated, respectable, and literate, and the wife, with her tablet and stylus, is shown as a full partner in that picture.

We'll imagine our Fortunata a little like her. She's not grand, but she's capable. She can read, she can count, and she keeps the business in order. In the morning, she'll be the one at the counter, taking the coins and chatting with the customers.

For now, though, she puts out the lamp by the bed, takes one last look at her sleeping children, and lies down to rest for a few hours. Down below, the night's work is moving on to the next stage.

28:53Making Roman Bread: Kneading, Shaping, and Stamping · 1,253 words

By the time the city is fully dark, the mills have made enough flour for the first part of the work. Secundus comes down the stairs, ties a cloth apron around his waist, and steps into the kneading room.

This room sits between the mills and the oven. It's cooler here, away from the fire, and the walls are lined with shelves. In the middle stands a large wooden trough for mixing the dough. Some Pompeian bakeries had something even more remarkable, a kneading machine. In several of them, archaeologists found round stone basins with holes in their sides for wooden paddles. A wooden shaft, turned by a person or perhaps an animal, stirred and folded the dough inside. It's an early example of a machine for making bread, and it saved a great deal of tired arms.

Our bakery is a little smaller though, and tonight the kneading is done by hand, in the long wooden trough. Into it go the flour, water from the street fountain or the house's cistern, and salt. And then there's the leaven.

Romans knew several ways to make bread rise. Pliny the Elder describes a few of them. One was to keep back a lump of dough from the day before, and let it go sour overnight, and then mix it into the new batch. That's the same idea as a sourdough starter today. Another was to use the froth from brewing, though Pliny says that was more of a custom in Gaul and Spain than in Italy. In a bakery like ours, a lump of yesterday's dough, kept in a covered bowl near the warm oven, is the most likely choice.

Secundus works the leaven into the flour and water. He pushes the heels of his palms into the dough, folds it, turns it, and pushes again. Two workers stand beside him, doing the same. It's slow rhythmic work. The dough starts out shaggy and sticky, and slowly turns smooth and springy. The men don't talk much. Now and then one of them hums a few lines of a song, and the others join in for a moment, and then let it fade.

When the dough is ready, it's covered with cloths and left to rest in the trough. The kneading room is warm from the oven next door, which helps the dough rise. Through the doorway, the glow of the oven paints a long soft stripe of orange across the floor.

While the dough rises, there's time to rest. The workers sit against the wall and close their eyes. The boy feeds the donkeys, and then takes a wooden bucket out to the corner fountain to fetch them water. Secundus checks the woodpile. He'll need plenty of it to heat the oven before dawn. Most of it is hardwood, brought in from the hills and stacked in neat piles under a lean-to roof. There are bundles of thin twigs too, for getting the fire going quickly.

Pompeii had around forty of these public fountains, spread through the town so that most people lived only a short walk from one. Each was a simple box of heavy stone blocks, with water pouring from a carved spout into the basin, day and night. The water came from an aqueduct that ran in from the hills, into a tall water tower near one of the town gates, and then through lead pipes under the pavements. Where people leaned on the edge of a basin to fill their jugs, the stone has been worn smooth and hollow, by countless hands and buckets over the years.

At night, the fountain is the only thing on the street still moving. The boy sets his bucket under the spout and listens to it fill, a clear, steady splash in the dark. Behind him, the bakery doorway shows a soft square of orange, the glow of the oven reaching out onto the paving stones. He carries the brimming bucket back carefully, and the donkeys drink, and nuzzle his shoulder, and settle again.

After an hour or two, the dough has risen nicely. Now comes the shaping. Each loaf is weighed out, more or less by eye, and then rolled into a round ball on a floury board. Secundus pats each one flat, into a thick disc, perhaps twenty centimetres across.

Then he does the thing that makes Pompeian bread so recognisable. He takes a thin wooden blade, or the back of a knife, and presses it deep into the top of the loaf, from one side to the other. He turns the loaf and does it again, and again, and once more, until the top is divided into eight equal wedges, like the spokes of a wheel. That's exactly the pattern you can see on the carbonized loaves from the bakery of Modestus. There's also a groove running around the side of many of them. For a long time, people thought a string was tied around the loaf before baking. But a recent study points out that no trace of string has ever been found, and suggests the groove simply came from the way the stiff dough was shaped.

Why the eight wedges? Most likely so that the loaf could be broken easily into portions, without a knife, at the table. One loaf, eight pieces, one for each person, or a few for each meal. The Romans sometimes called this kind of loaf panis quadratus, which sounds as though it ought to mean square bread. It probably refers to the way the top was divided, first in half, and then into quarters, not to the shape of the loaf itself.

Last of all comes the stamp. Some Roman bakers pressed a small stamp into the dough before baking. It might be made of bronze or clay or wood, and it carried a name, or a mark. One carbonized loaf found at Herculaneum, the neighbouring town along the bay, still carries a stamp naming a man called Celer, the slave of Quintus Granius Verus. It may have shown who made the loaf, or who owned the bakery, or whose household had ordered it. Some households brought their own dough to be baked, and a stamp would make sure the right loaves went back home.

Secundus presses his stamp into each loaf, one after the other. The wooden handle is smooth and dark from years of use. The mark is small and neat, just a few raised letters. Then each loaf is set on a long wooden board, dusted with flour, and covered with a cloth to rise again, one last time.

There are dozens of them now, row after row, on boards stacked on racks along the wall. In the low light, they look like smooth pale river stones. The kneading room smells of yeast and flour, and very faintly of the woodsmoke drifting in from the oven room.

Secundus wipes his hands on his apron and steps out into the courtyard for some air. The night is clear and warm. Above the roof tiles, the stars are thick and bright, the way they only are in a town with no streetlights. The donkeys have stopped walking now. The mills are still. And for a little while, the bakery is quiet.

He leans in the doorway, breathes in the night air, and lets his eyes close for a moment. There's an hour or so before the oven needs heating. So let's leave him there, and take a slow walk through the sleeping town.

37:50A Walk Through the Sleeping Town · 1,334 words

Let's step out of the bakery door and onto the street. It's very dark. There are no street lamps in Pompeii. Anyone out at night would carry a small oil lamp in a clay holder, or a torch, or would simply walk by starlight, keeping close to the walls.

The town at night isn't completely silent though. Romans often complained about the noise of their cities after dark. In Rome itself, wheeled carts were mostly banned from the streets in the daytime, so deliveries rumbled through at night. The poet Juvenal joked that the only people who could sleep in Rome were the rich. Pompeii is much smaller and quieter than Rome, but even here, the night has its sounds.

A cart rolls by, slowly, its iron-rimmed wheels clattering over the paving stones and bumping over the stepping stones at the crossing. It's carrying amphorae of wine, the tall clay jars with pointed bottoms, packed in straw. The driver nods to us as he passes. Further on, we hear the soft murmur of voices from a tavern that's still open. A few men are sitting at a counter, drinking a last cup of wine and playing a game of dice. On the wall outside, someone has scratched a few words into the plaster. Pompeii's walls are covered with these little scratched notes, called graffiti, and they're one of the most charming things about the town.

That same tavern, in the block of Popidius Priscus, had a price list of sorts scratched on its wall. It speaks in the voice of a woman named Hedone, and it says that here you can drink for one as. If you pay two, you'll drink better wine. And if you pay four, you can drink Falernian, one of the most famous wines in Italy. We don't know if Hedone ran the bar, or if her name was just part of the joke. But it's a rare chance to hear a Pompeian shopkeeper's sales pitch, almost in her own words.

Across the street, a food bar is closing for the night. Pompeii had more than a hundred and fifty places like it, with counters facing the street. A study of the town's shops found that they made up more than a quarter of all the shops in Pompeii. The counter is built of masonry, faced with odd pieces of coloured marble, and set into its top are big clay jars for food and drink. A young woman is scrubbing out the jars with a cloth and a bucket of water. She stacks the cups on a shelf at the end of the counter and pulls the wooden shutters across, board by board, until only a thin line of lamplight shows between them. Then that goes out too.

One of these bars, found only a few years ago, has a counter painted with bright pictures. There's a sea nymph riding a sea horse, a pair of ducks hung up ready for the pot, a rooster, and a little scene that seems to show the shop itself. Somebody wanted their counter to look cheerful, and to tell passers-by, at a glance, what was on offer.

People wrote all sorts of things. There are greetings to friends, and notes about debts, and lines of poetry. There are lists of prices and the dates when something happened. There are even love notes. One person wrote that he'd had dinner here, and another simply wrote that a certain Gaius was here, the way people still do today. One famous scratched line, found in more than one place, wonders at how the walls haven't fallen down under the weight of so much nonsense written on them.

We walk on, past the dark doorways of houses. Some of the larger houses have a heavy wooden door, closed now and barred from the inside. If you could look through, you'd see an atrium, a tall central hall with an opening in the roof to let in light and rain. Below the opening, a shallow pool, called the impluvium, collects the rainwater and feeds it into a cistern underground. Tonight, a few stars are reflected in the still water.

We step carefully across the street on the tall stepping stones. In the dark, you have to feel for them with your feet. Between them, the paving is worn into deep grooves by the iron rims of cart wheels, and the stones themselves are polished smooth by years of feet. Carts had to line their wheels up with the gaps between the stepping stones to get through. In some places the grooves are so deep that you can still lay your hand in them today.

A little further on, we pass a grand house belonging to a man named Siricus, one of the town's well-known citizens. Set into the floor of his entrance hall is a small mosaic, two words in black and white tiles, greeting everyone who comes in. They mean, roughly, welcome, profit. It's a very Pompeian greeting, cheerful and businesslike, and it suits a town that lived by trade. His house stands in the same block as the bakery of Modestus, only a short walk away.

Beyond the atrium, in the finest houses, there are gardens surrounded by columns, with small fountains, bronze statues, and beds of herbs and flowers. The scent of the plants drifts out into the warm night air, rosemary and myrtle, and perhaps a few late roses.

But most of Pompeii's people didn't live in grand houses. They lived in small rooms above shops, like our baker's family, or in back rooms behind workshops, or in little rented apartments. Many of them didn't have kitchens of their own. That's one reason there were so many bakeries and food bars in town. People bought their bread fresh every morning, and a hot meal at a counter when they could afford it.

We come out into the Forum, the great open square at the heart of the town. It's long and paved with pale stone, and it's lined with colonnades on three sides. At the northern end, the temple of Jupiter rises on its high platform. Behind it, far away and dark against the starry sky, is the long soft outline of the mountain.

To the people of Pompeii, Vesuvius was simply a mountain. It was green and fertile, with vineyards and woods on its lower slopes, and a broad flat top. A painting found in a Pompeian house shows the god of wine standing beside a tall green mountain covered in vines, and many scholars think it's Vesuvius. The Romans of this time didn't think of it as a volcano at all. The Greek geographer Strabo, writing a few generations earlier, noticed that the rocks near its summit looked burnt, as though fire had once been there. But for the people of the town, it was the place where their wine came from.

The Forum is empty now. A cat slips across the paving stones and vanishes into a doorway. In the colonnade, a man is asleep on a bench, wrapped in his cloak, perhaps a traveller who arrived too late to find a room. The great bronze statues on their bases stand quietly in the dark.

The town is very still. Most of its people are asleep. The fishermen down at the harbour will be up before long, and the farmers outside the walls will rise with the first grey light. But for now, the only ones awake are a few late travellers, the last few drinkers in the taverns, and the bakers.

And if you stand very still in the middle of the Forum and breathe in, you might catch it on the night air, faint at first, and then stronger, from several directions at once. It's woodsmoke. Across the town, in bakery after bakery, the fires are being stirred back to life.

Let's turn around and walk slowly back through the dark streets, toward the warm doorway on the corner.

47:39The Pompeii Bakery Oven Before Dawn · 990 words

Back in the bakery, the glow of the oven is growing brighter. Secundus has raked the ashes open, and laid a bundle of dry twigs on the embers, and then thicker pieces of wood on top. The fire catches, crackles, and climbs. Soon the whole oven is roaring softly, and the room is filled with flickering orange light.

A Pompeian bread oven is a beautiful piece of work. It's built of brick and stone, and it's shaped like a low dome, or a beehive. The floor of the oven is flat, and made of smooth stone or tile, and it's raised to about the height of a man's waist, so the baker doesn't have to bend too far. At the front is an arched opening, with a stone shelf in front of it, and above that is a sort of front chamber with a flue, to carry the smoke up and away. Many Pompeian ovens are still standing today, their domes cracked but whole, their mouths blackened by the fires of long ago.

The baking method is simple and very old. You don't bake with the fire still burning. Instead, you build a hot fire inside the oven, right on its floor, and let it burn until the dome and floor have soaked up all the heat they can hold. That takes an hour or two. The bricks of the dome go from dark to dull red, and then pale, as the soot burns off them. A baker could tell by the colour when the oven was ready.

While the fire burns, one of the workers goes round the room refilling the lamps. Roman oil lamps were small closed clay vessels, about the size of a palm, with a round hole on top for pouring in the oil, and a short nozzle at the front for the wick. They burned olive oil, and the wick was a twist of linen or plant fibre. Thousands of them have been found at Pompeii, many made in moulds, with little pictures pressed into their tops, of gods and animals, gladiators and ships. In a bakery, they'd be set in niches in the walls and on shelves, wherever someone needed to see. Each one gives only a small steady flame. But tonight, beside the oven, they hardly seem to matter. The whole room is lit by the fire.

While the fire burns, the workers carry the boards of risen loaves in from the kneading room and set them down near the oven. In many Pompeian bakeries, there's a small window or hatch in the wall between the kneading room and the oven room, so the boards could be passed through without carrying them the long way round. The loaves have risen nicely under their cloths. They're puffy and soft, and the eight lines on top have spread a little wider.

At last, Secundus decides the oven is ready. He takes a long iron rake and pulls the glowing embers out of the oven, into a stone channel or a pit at the front. Then, as wood-fired bakers still do today, he takes a mop made of wet rags tied to a pole, and sweeps the oven floor clean of ash. The rags hiss and steam as they touch the hot stone. The smell of damp hot brick fills the room.

Now the loaves go in. Secundus uses a long wooden peel, a flat paddle with a long handle. He slides it under a loaf, lifts it, and pushes it deep into the back of the oven with one smooth movement. Then he pulls the peel out, leaving the loaf behind on the hot floor. Another loaf, and another, row after row, working from the back toward the front, until the oven floor is covered.

When the oven is full, he closes the mouth with a door of iron. That's exactly how the oven at the bakery of Modestus was found, closed with an iron door, with its eighty-one loaves still inside. Now the trapped heat in the dome and the floor does the work. The bread bakes slowly and evenly, rising in the heat, its crust turning golden brown.

Nobody hurries now. The workers sit down on benches against the wall, wipe their faces, and drink some water mixed with a little wine. The boy has fallen asleep on a pile of empty sacks in the corner, his arm around his knees. Secundus stands by the oven, watching the edges of the iron door, where a thin line of light glows around its rim.

The boy in the corner sleeps on. He's been up since before dawn yesterday, leading the donkeys and carrying grain, and now he's curled on the sacks with flour in his hair. Someone has laid a rough wool cloak over him. In a bakery like this, a boy like him might well have been enslaved, owned by the baker, or by the man who owned the building. We don't know his name, and history usually doesn't record names like his at all. But for tonight, let's imagine him warm, and fed, and sleeping deeply, with the glow of the oven on his face. In the stable beside him, the donkeys are asleep too, standing with their heads low and one hind hoof tipped up, the way donkeys often rest.

And then the smell begins. First it's just a hint, warm and nutty, slipping out around the edge of the door. Then it grows and fills the room, and spills out into the courtyard, and drifts through the open doorway into the street. It's the smell of baking bread, the same smell that's filled bakeries for thousands of years, from Egypt to Gaul, and from Pompeii to the kitchen down the road from you.

In the stable, the old brown donkey lifts his head and sniffs the air. Upstairs, Fortunata stirs in her sleep, and smiles a little, and turns over.

54:41The Town Wakes · 688 words

After a while, Secundus opens the door. A great wave of heat and steam rolls out. He reaches in with the peel and draws out a loaf. He taps the bottom with his knuckle and listens. It sounds hollow. It's done.

One by one, the loaves come out, golden brown and crackling, their eight wedges standing up proud, the stamp pressed neatly into each one. They're set on racks and shelves to cool. Some of them will go out to the shop counter. Others are packed into wide flat baskets, to be carried out to customers around the town.

In the east, the sky is beginning to pale. The stars fade one by one. A cock crows somewhere nearby, and then another, further away. Romans divided the daylight into twelve hours, from sunrise to sunset, so in summer the first hour started very early indeed. And everywhere, the bakers had to be ready before it.

The poet Martial, writing in Rome at about this time, made a little joke on this theme. Get up, he tells some boys. The baker's already selling breakfast. He was talking about Rome, but it might as well have been Pompeii.

Fortunata comes down the stairs, tying back her hair. She opens the wooden shutters of the shop, one board at a time, and sets out the fresh loaves on the counter. The street outside is grey and cool, and already there are people about. A slave from a big house up the hill comes to collect the household's order. A young man on his way to work buys a single small loaf and eats it as he walks. A woman with a baby on her hip buys two loaves and a little extra for her neighbour.

A little later, the regulars begin to arrive. There's an old man who always buys the darker cheaper bread, and asks after the children. There's a cook from a food bar down the street, who takes a whole basket for her counter. And there's a woman from the house up the hill, who hands over a covered board of her own dough. She made it at home last night, and it carries her household's stamp. The baker will bake it in his oven for a small fee, and she'll come back for it later in the morning. That was common in Roman towns. Not everyone had an oven, but almost everyone could make dough.

Out in the street, the light is coming up grey and gold. Shutters are sliding open, one after another, all along the pavement. The food bar across the way is lighting its brazier. A cart creaks past with vegetables from the farms outside the walls. And from the bakery door, the warm smell of bread drifts out into the morning, the last of the oven's glow, mixing now with sunlight.

There's a painting from Pompeii that shows a scene very much like this. A man sits behind a wooden counter piled high with round loaves, each scored into wedges, and he hands bread to a small group of customers. Scholars still argue about what it shows. It might be an ordinary bread seller, or it might be a public handout of bread from a man running for office. Either way, it's a lovely glimpse of the round loaves we've been watching all night, being handed across a counter to people who'll eat them that day.

The coins clink into Fortunata's bowl. She marks the sales on her wax tablet. The children come down, rubbing their eyes, and she gives them each a warm wedge of bread, broken from a fresh loaf, with a little olive oil to dip it in.

And Secundus? He's finally done. He washes his face and arms at the courtyard basin, and climbs the narrow stairs. He lies down on his bed as the sunlight comes up over the rooftops of Pompeii. Downstairs, the mills will start turning again soon, and the day's next batch of dough will be mixed, and in the evening, the glow of the oven will rise again. But for now, the baker sleeps.

59:43Goodnight in Pompeii · 281 words

We know so much about this one ordinary night because of what happened to Pompeii years later, in seventy-nine CE, when the mountain behind the town buried it under ash. That's why the mills and the ovens, and even the loaves, are still there for us to see. But the people who lived here didn't know that, and tonight we don't need to think about it either. For them, this was just another night, and another morning, with bread on the table.

Tonight, we've been a long way. From a bakers' street at dusk, with its painted notices and its late drinkers, to the mill room, where the donkeys walked their slow circles. From a quiet supper by the household shrine to the kneading trough and the bread stamps. Through the sleeping town, past dark doorways and closed shutters, and back to the oven before dawn. And all of it, in the end, was a story about bread, and the people who stayed awake to make it.

Now, it's time to rest. The night is here for you. Let the rumble of the mills slow and fade. Let the donkeys doze in their stable, and the shutters stay closed along the street. Let the glow of the oven settle into soft red embers, and the long night of bread come quietly to its end.

You don't need to do anything now. Nothing to remember. Nothing to finish. You can let the day go, like flour settling on a quiet floor, one soft drift at a time. And in Pompeii, the baker sleeps, a warm loaf rests on the counter, and the whole street is still.

Goodnight. Until next time, sleep well.
